content: The monkeypox virus, also referred to as MPOX, was first identified in 1958 in monkeys that were transported from Singapore to Denmark. The initial human case of monkeypox was documented in 1970 in the Republic of the Congo, involving a hospitalized child. Monkeypox belongs to the orthopoxvirus genus within the Poxviridae family. The virus is capable of being transmitted through animal-to-animal, animal-to-human, and human-to-human interactions. However, there is limited evidence to support mother-to-child transmission. The historical emergence of monkeypox began with its identification in monkeys in 1958. The first human case was reported in 1970 in the Republic of the Congo. Over the subsequent years, cases were recorded in 11 African countries, with more than 400 cases documented by the late 1980s. A significant decline in reported cases occurred in the early 1990s, with no cases reported between 1993 and 1995. In 1996, an outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo led to a large number of suspected cases, though only a small number were confirmed through laboratory testing. In 2003, the United States reported 47 confirmed and probable cases of monkeypox. In the years that followed, sporadic cases were identified in non-endemic regions, primarily in the United Kingdom and Singapore, all of which were linked to travel from endemic areas. In May 2022, clusters of monkeypox cases were identified globally within a short timeframe. By May 22, 2022, 109 confirmed cases and 87 suspected cases were reported worldwide. By June 2, 2022, the World Health Organization (WHO) had identified or received reports of 780 cases. As of June 15, 2022, a total of 2,103 laboratory-confirmed cases, including one death, had been reported to the WHO. The monkeypox virus is a member of the orthopoxvirus genus and has a genome composed of linear double-stranded DNA, which replicates in the cytoplasm of infected cells. There are two genetic clades of the virus: the West African clade and the Central African (Congo Basin) clade. The potential role of vaginal fluids and semen in transmission is still under investigation. Direct contact with lesions or bodily fluids of an infected animal can also result in transmission. Human-to-human transmission occurs through close physical contact with an infected individual, including direct contact with lesions, bodily fluids, respiratory secretions, or contaminated materials. Transmission via the placenta from mother to fetus is also possible. The differential diagnosis for monkeypox includes smallpox, chickenpox, scabies, syphilis, bacterial skin infections, and drug-associated allergic reactions. The precise prevalence and incidence of monkeypox are challenging to determine due to underreporting in past outbreaks. In the 1970s and 1980s, the median age of infection was 4 to 5 years. By the 2000s and 2010s, the median age had increased to 10 to 21 years. In May 2022, the average median age of monkeypox infections was 37 years. Monkeypox is generally a self-limiting disease, with symptoms resolving within 2 to 4 weeks. Complications are rare but can include secondary bacterial infections such as pneumonia, sepsis, encephalitis, corneal inflammation, and conjunctivitis. Key historical and symptomatic information for diagnosis includes recent travel to endemic areas or potential contact with infected individuals, animals, or contaminated materials. Initial symptoms include fever, chills, lymphadenopathy, headache, and myalgia, followed by a skin rash with multiple lesions that evolve simultaneously. The progression of lesions typically follows this timeline: macular (1–2 days), papular (1–2 days), vesicular (1–2 days), pustular (5–7 days), and scab formation (7–14 days). Physical examination findings depend on the disease stage and may include low-grade fever, enlarged lymph nodes (submental, submandibular, cervical, inguinal), and a skin rash with the characteristic progression of lesions. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing is the preferred diagnostic method for confirming monkeypox virus due to its high sensitivity and accuracy. Samples should be collected from skin lesions, specifically from the roof or fluid of vesicles and pustules, as well as dry crusts. PCR testing of blood is generally inconclusive because the virus does not persist in the bloodstream for long. There are no electrocardiogram (EKG) findings associated with monkeypox. Ultrasound may be useful for assessing fetal well-being in pregnant women with confirmed monkeypox. Currently, there is no proven or safe treatment specifically for monkeypox. To control outbreaks, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends the use of the smallpox vaccine, cidofovir, ST-246, and vaccinia immune globulin. Vaccines are not yet available to the general public, but in the event of a larger outbreak, the CDC will provide guidelines on vaccine distribution. Surgical intervention is not indicated for monkeypox, as it is typically a self-limiting disease with symptoms lasting 2 to 4 weeks. The CDC advises proper hand hygiene using soap and water or alcohol-based hand sanitizers after contact with infected individuals or animals. Avoiding contact with animals that may serve as reservoirs for the virus, such as rodents, is recommended. Additionally, individuals should avoid close contact with lesions, bodily fluids, respiratory droplets, or contaminated materials such as bedding or towels. Healthcare workers should use personal protective equipment (PPE) when managing patients, and infected individuals should be isolated to prevent further spread.
